cards.text: This one's a song of ascents, baker. The psalmist looks up at the hills and asks one big question: "From where does my help come?"

cards.question: The psalmist is staring up at the hills and asking where help comes from. What's the answer?
The LORD who helps the psalmist is the One who made the hills the psalmist is looking at.

cards.text: The Maker of heaven and earth. Friend, that's skipping the help desk and going straight to the One who built the WHOLE building!
Now the psalm switches from my to your. And it starts right down at the ground, with your feet.

cards.question: The psalm starts with your feet. What does it say the LORD won't let your foot do?

cards.text: Then the psalm tells you something about your Protector. It says it once, then turns right around and says it again with more.

cards.question: The Protector in this psalm needs a little rest now and then.

cards.text: The Protector of Israel will neither slumber nor sleep. Me, I closed my eyes for ONE minute next to the oven and woke up to a tray of cookie-shaped charcoal.
Then the psalm says it plain: the LORD is your keeper. And it paints a picture too: the LORD is the shade on your right hand.

cards.question: With the LORD as your shade, the ___ will not strike you by day.
This psalm says the LORD's protection stops when the day ends.

cards.text: Feet, sun, moon. Now the psalm stops going piece by piece and goes BIG.

cards.question: The psalm goes big: the LORD will guard you from ___ evil.
Besides guarding you from evil, what does the psalm say the LORD will preserve?

cards.text: Last line: the LORD will watch over your coming and going. Friend, I spent YEARS in a junk drawer with no comings and NO goings, and He's watching over every single one of yours!

cards.question: The LORD watches over your coming and going. For how long?

findings.problem: The statement says the Protector 'needs a little rest now and then,' but Psalm 121:3-4 says He will not 'slumber' and will 'neither slumber nor sleep.' 'Rest' is a different, broader word. Genesis 2:2 says God rested on the seventh day, so a baker could argue the right answer. The card should use the psalm's own words, slumber or sleep.

rule.text: Call things what the text calls them.

findings.problem: 'Feet, sun, moon' treats the moon as something the baker has already been told. No card ever tells the second half of Psalm 121:6, 'nor the moon by night.' Card 12 only asks whether protection stops when the day ends. The baker leaves Prep without that detail ever being told.

rule.text: When the baker leaves Prep, they understand the whole passage without missing an important detail.

findings.problem: The right answer, 'Now and forevermore,' sounds like the Bible. The wrong answers, 'Only while you travel' and 'Until you reach home,' sound modern. They also start with limiting words that mark them as wrong.

rule.text: Don't let the right answer stand out. All the answers should sound alike. None should sound more like the Bible, or more modern, than the others.
